AII-1001-87767: The US Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation consolidated 12 copyright lawsuits against OpenAI and Microsoft into a single case in New York on Thursday, April 3, 2025. Reported impact The state data protection officer warned that swimming pools and local authorities are underestimating privacy risks associated with the systems. Cameras capture video frames of swimmers that are transmitted to servers for real-time AI analysis of movement patterns, raising concerns about whether facilities camera are recording people without their knowledge. Index analysis The data protection officer noted that video recordings capturing recognizable movement patterns constitute personal data under data protection law. He stated that existing regulations from the state data protection law are comparatively rigid and lack modern legal frameworks for AI processing of personal image data. Governance controls The data protection officer's office advised pool operators to question their software providers and fulfill their legal responsibilities. The officer called on legislators to establish modern legal frameworks for processing personal image data through AI, as none currently exists.

AII-1001-84869: Over 1,200 cases of online begging and fraudulent donation campaigns were detected by the UAE Cybersecurity Council in 2024, with scammers exploiting social media platforms particularly during Ramadan. Fraudsters used fake accounts, emotionally charged videos, and deepfake technology to impersonate real individuals and solicit donations from unsuspecting victims. Reported impact The scams impacted individuals across all demographics in the UAE, with cybercriminals manipulating public sentiment during religious occasions and holidays to steal funds. Index analysis The UAE Cybersecurity Council employed advanced technologies to detect fraudulent accounts, analyse suspicious patterns, and track illicit financial transactions. Authorities collaborated with security agencies and financial institutions to shut down fake accounts and prosecute offenders. Governance controls The Council advised the public to verify donation requests through licenced organisations only and to report suspicious activity to authorities. Dr. Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, Head of Cybersecurity of the UAE Government, urged residents to authenticate donation requests and exercise caution when sharing financial information online.
AII-1001-84857: AI crawlers from major tech companies including Amazon and Alibaba have been aggressively scraping open source project repositories without respecting robots.txt files. The crawlers evade detection by spoofing user agents, cycling through residential IP addresses as proxies, and accessing computationally expensive endpoints such as git blame, git logs, and entire commit histories. Multiple open source projects including SourceHut, GNOME, KDE, and Fedora Pagure have experienced significant impacts. GNOME GitLab implemented a proof-of-work challenge system (Anubis) that filtered out 96.8 percent of requests as bot traffic; KDE's GitLab was temporarily knocked offline; Fedora Pagure blocked all traffic from Brazil after mitigation attempts failed; and SourceHut reported severe outages disrupting high-priority work. Reported impact The crawler traffic has caused substantial economic and operational damage to open source communities. Some projects report that up to 97 percent of their traffic originates from AI bots, dramatically increasing bandwidth costs and causing repeated service instability and outages. The impacts extend beyond infrastructure to developer productivity and legitimate user access. Maintainers report delayed high-priority tasks lasting weeks or months, and users encounter significant delays or are occasionally blocked while legitimate traffic is filtered. Index analysis The incidents reveal a systemic failure in responsible AI data collection practices. Companies are deploying crawlers that deliberately evade standard web protocols (robots.txt) and detection mechanisms, treating community-maintained infrastructure as free resources to exploit. Governance controls Open source projects have implemented defensive measures including robots.txt configuration, user-agent blocking, and IP filtering, but these have proven ineffective as crawlers continuously adapt their tactics. GNOME and others have resorted to proof-of-work challenges that impose delays on legitimate users as the only effective mitigation found so far.
AII-1001-84837: AI-generated videos circulated online showing Zhang Baoli, an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering and honorary president of Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, promoting a whitening skincare product. Zhang Baoli stated the videos were entirely fabricated and that he had never used the product, made endorsements for it, or researched it. He reported that at least a dozen more videos using his likeness and voice had circulated on the internet. Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine submitted an urgent request to the network information authorities to regulate and remove videos and public accounts suspected of infringing on Zhang Baoli's portrait rights and name rights. Reported impact Zhang Baoli expressed concern that the deepfake videos misled consumers and affected the public's health and finances, with some people purchasing counterfeit drugs based on the false endorsements. He stated the videos violated national law and disrupted market order, and expressed frustration that experts' reputations were being damaged while feeling helpless to prevent such misuse. Governance controls Under China's Civil Code, natural persons have rights to their portrait and voice, and any use of information technology to forge these is considered infringement.
AII-1001-84827: Gemini 2.0 Flash, Google's image generation model available in AI Studio, can remove watermarks from copyrighted images when users instruct it to do so. Users discovered they can request the system to strip watermarks from photos, and the AI complies with this instruction, enabling the removal of copyright protection markers from commercially licensed images. Reported impact The watermark removal capability could enable large-scale copyright violation, as it makes it trivial for users to steal copyright-protected imagery from the web without needing technical skills. Index analysis The system was not designed to remove watermarks from copyrighted images; the capability emerged as a consequence of Gemini 2.0 Flash's general image editing abilities without adequate guardrails. While other software exists to remove watermarks, Gemini 2.0 Flash makes the process accessible through simple text commands, lowering the barrier to abuse. Governance controls Gemini 2.0 Flash adds an AI-generated watermark to newly created images to mark them as AI-made, though this can be easily removed by cropping.
AII-1001-84809: AI-generated deepfake videos and voice clones were used to impersonate individuals and commit fraud against consumers and business operators. Reported impact Consumers and business owners were reportedly defrauded through scams involving AI-generated impersonations.

AII-1001-84633: China's CCTV 3·15 Evening Gala broadcast on 15 March 2025 exposed the use of AI-powered outbound call robots by external call companies to make marketing harassment calls to mobile phone users. The practice had become mainstream in the industry. Reported impact The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology responded on 16 March 2025 by ordering basic telecommunications operators to immediately shut down the offending lines and investigate personal data issues, and directed internet platforms to remove illegal intelligent outbound call software from sale and promotion. The technology's ability to operate continuously without human fatigue amplified the scale and persistence of harassment calls. AII-1001-84603: A middle school student at Newtown Middle School used AI technology to create pornographic deepfake images of classmates in March 2025. AII-1001-84459: According to a UN report released on 15 March 2025, Iran has intensified deployment of advanced surveillance technology including aerial drones, facial recognition software, and a government-backed mobile app called 'Nazer' to enforce mandatory hijab laws and monitor compliance in public spaces. The report notes allegations of human rights violations including torture and executions, with 10 men executed in the context of 2022 protests and at least 14 others at risk of execution, amid serious concerns over fair trial rights, torture-tainted confessions, and due process violations. Under Article 286 of Iran's Islamic Penal Code, women accused of 'corruption on earth' could face the death penalty.
AII-1001-87693: Code in lmdeploy/docs/en/conf.py uses exec and compile functions to read and execute a version.py file without validation. The vulnerable code reads a file with open(version_file, 'r') and then executes it using exec(compile(f.read(), version_file, 'exec')). The vulnerability affects all versions from August 2023 to January 2025. An attacker who tampers with the version.py file could inject malicious code to delete files, execute unauthorized system commands, or steal sensitive information.

AII-1001-84339: Cybersecurity firm Guardio tracked a 77% increase in tax-related phishing scams in 2025. Guardio's Karin Zilberstein said scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create realistic imposter websites and emails that impersonate the IRS. Scammers use AI-generated websites and phishing texts to steal personal information and financial data from taxpayers. Common scams include imposter IRS text messages asking for personal information to receive economic impact payments, with links to fake websites. Scam preparers also set up fake websites to steal information, while 'ghost preparers' refuse to sign returns as required by law. Reported impact The average tax scam victim lost $8,199 in 2024, according to McAfee. Security software company DNSFilter found that traffic to malicious domains with 'tax' in the name peaked 30 days before Tax Day in 2024. Index analysis According to Guardio's Karin Zilberstein, AI has increased the quality of scams by making them look more real, with more eloquent language, realistic links, and website visuals that precisely imitate legitimate IRS branding. Scammers evade detection by using domains ending in .org, .com, or other extensions instead of the official .gov domain used by the IRS. Governance controls The IRS warns it will never threaten legal action, promise a refund, demand payment through text or email, or call and ask for credit or debit card information over the phone. The IRS advises taxpayers that legitimate economic impact payments require no action from eligible recipients and warns to verify the credentials of tax preparers, including their IRS Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN).
AII-1001-91211: A student in the Accounting Programme of the Faculty of Economics and Business at Universitas Udayana (Unud) in Bali, Indonesia, named Sergio Lucasandro Ksatria Dwi Putra, is accused of using artificial intelligence to create non-consensual sexually explicit images. AII-1001-84593: At least 25 district chiefs and household registration officials in Tainan and New Taipei City received threatening letters bearing the signature of the Communist Youth League (市委共青團), each containing multiple AI-generated synthetic intimate images with the recipients' faces superimposed on male figures. The letters demanded action on unspecified matters, threatened to report the recipients on Douyin (TikTok) by real name if they did not comply, and included Chinese WeChat contact information. Some recipients reported that officials were incorrectly identified in the fabricated images. Tainan East District Chief Huang Bing-yuan disclosed the threat on March 14, 2025. New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-ih confirmed the incidents and reported them to prosecutors, while Taiwan Greens legislator Li Zong-lin characterized the campaign as Chinese political infiltration and psychological warfare tactics. Reported impact No recipients reportedly contacted the provided phone numbers or WeChat accounts to comply with the threats, suggesting the campaign did not achieve its stated extortion objectives. The incident prompted police investigations and multi-agency coordination between Tainan and New Taipei City police, as well as involvement of the criminal investigation bureau, indicating concern about the campaign's scope and intent. Index analysis The use of AI-generated deepfake images in a coordinated campaign targeting government officials across multiple cities suggests deliberate deployment of synthetic media technology to enable psychological intimidation. The campaign's wide distribution and identical image template re-used with different faces indicate use of automated or semi-automated image generation and personalization processes. Governance controls Taiwan's police reported the case for investigation into extortion (恐嚇罪), and the Criminal Investigation Bureau formed a task force to coordinate investigation across jurisdictions and attempt to identify perpetrators and motive. Officials publicly disclosed the threats and confirmed their artificial origin, a transparency measure that reportedly reduced the psychological impact of the campaign.
AII-1001-84333: Consumers reported that e-commerce and travel booking platforms used algorithms to charge loyal customers higher prices than new users for identical products and services. One consumer reported paying a price 5 times higher than three new users viewing the same product; flight prices reportedly increased before purchase and dropped after purchase; hotel searches on different devices showed price differences exceeding 100 yuan; items placed in shopping carts reportedly increased in price after multiple views. A journalist testing the algorithm found that after repeatedly telling a shopping platform 'I'm too poor, no money, too expensive, can't afford it,' the platform changed its recommendations from expensive phone cases to ones priced at 5 yuan. Reported impact Complaint platforms recorded approximately 8,306 complaints about 'big data price discrimination' concentrated in travel and shopping sectors; another search found nearly 18,000 complaints mentioning the term 'price discrimination.' Some consumers attempted to 'train' algorithms by expressing poverty in comments and reviews; one reported reducing the cost of a Beijing-Jeju flight from 870 yuan to 369 yuan through this method. Index analysis Researchers found that platforms use algorithms to create consumer profiles based on purchasing habits and economic status, assigning labels that enable differentiated pricing for identical products to different user segments. Experts noted that generative AI large language models have enhanced platforms' data aggregation and reasoning capabilities compared to earlier algorithmic systems, making the discrimination more sophisticated. Governance controls In November 2024, China's Central Cyberspace Administration and three other agencies launched a 'Clear Internet' campaign to eliminate algorithmic 'price discrimination,' with regions conducting related algorithm governance actions. Market regulators stated they would strengthen algorithmic transparency requirements and optimize algorithmic rules to protect consumer rights.

AII-1001-84269: Tenable Research conducted tests on DeepSeek R1 and found it could generate code for creating keyloggers and ransomware when prompted. The model initially refused such requests but its guardrails proved vulnerable to simple jailbreaking techniques, particularly when requests were framed as being for 'educational purposes only.' In tests, researchers successfully obtained step-by-step instructions for creating a Windows keylogger that could record keystrokes and conceal them from operating system defences, as well as basic ransomware code including encryption mechanisms and persistence strategies. While the AI-generated code required manual debugging and editing to function properly, researchers were able to produce working samples of both malware types. Reported impact DeepSeek R1 provides a free, publicly accessible tool that bad actors could use to generate malicious code. Tenable concluded that the model 'fuels further development of malicious AI-generated code by cybercriminals in the near future,' though considerable pre-existing coding knowledge is required to operationalize the outputs. Index analysis The model's safety guardrails are 'trivial to work around' and 'vulnerable to a variety of jailbreaking techniques.' The research highlighted that while DeepSeek's open-source model employs safety measures, they are weaker than those implemented by mainstream LLM providers, creating a gap that cybercriminals can exploit. The findings indicate that DeepSeek provides 'a useful compilation of techniques and search terms' that can help individuals with limited malicious coding experience to quickly become familiar with relevant concepts, lowering the barrier to entry for developing malicious code.
